newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africans face wait for details of Biko's death.
newsitem.headline: S.Africans face wait for details of Biko's death.

text.p: Five former policemen have confessed to beating anti-apartheid icon Steve Biko to death in 1977, but it could be months before they are called on to tell the nation why they did it, and on whose orders.

The five announced through their lawyer on Tuesday that they would seek amnesty from Archbishop Desmond Tutu's statutory Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) for killing Biko while he was detained in an apartheid prison.

TRC spokesman John Allen said on Wednesday the ex-policemen would have to take their place in a queue of over 4,500 people seeking amnesty for politically motivated crimes committed in the struggle over apartheid.
"We are legally obliged to give precedence to people who are in prison. It will be a number of months before we hear public testimony about how Biko died," he explained.
He said the TRC investigative unit would examine the evidence submitted by Biko's killers and would determine whether they had met the requirement for full disclosure.
White Afrikaner legislator Nic Koornhof told Reuters the confession that Biko was killed and did not die as a result of any accident was not unexpected, but had still come as a shock.
"I was not surprised because I think I knew all along that he was killed by police, but there was still a feeling of shock and deep disappointment. That was my gut reaction," he said.
"The big question is going to be why they killed Biko...It would be fair to them and to the nation to see the chain of command. Someone was thinking up the orders they followed."
Koornhof said the truth commission, which has been at work for a little over a year, had forced most Afrikaners to accept that terrible things were done in their name under apartheid.
"So many people just looked the other way - myself, the churches, all of us," he said.
Biko's widow, Ntsiki, and the wives of others whose deaths were explained in the latest batch of amnesty applications have declined to comment on the process.
But the Biko family made their opposition to the exchange of pardon for information known in an unsuccessful application to the Constitutional Court last year to halt the process.
"I think it is an extremely shabby state of affairs," said a lawyer who was involved in the application on Wednesday.

"The families of people who were butchered by a fascist regime are denied the redress under our new democratic government that they would have had even under the old regime if they had been able to prove their case," he said.

University of Cape Town political scientist Robert Schrire said pardons for Biko's killers and last year's amnesty for policeman Brian Mitchell, who organised the slaughter of 11 black men, women and children in 1988, probably would be the toughest tests of the reconciliation process.

"We had the ultimate brutality in Mitchell's case. Now we have the ultimate celebrity in Biko. He was the Mandela of his time. Had he lived, there is no doubt he would have played a leading role in this government," he said.

Schrire said the only other case that could strain South Africa's commitment to forgiveness would be the amnesty applications of two white right-wingers who assassinated popular Communist Party leader Chris Hani in 1993.

Former Conservative Party legislator Clive Derby-Lewis and Polish immigrant Janus Walusz, both serving life sentences for Hani's killing, have applied for amnesty on the grounds that their actions were politically motivated.
"There is more doubt about them getting amnesty than about most of the others," Schrire said.
